tts: Tonight, millions of kids will ring doorbells dressed as ghosts, witches and skeletons. Americans will spend about thirteen and a half billion dollars on Halloween this year: around four billion on costumes, four on decorations, and four on candy. But this holiday didn't start with candy. It started more than a thousand years ago, with something much darker: the fear that on one night a year, the dead come back. So, where did Halloween actually come from? Let's travel back in time.

Our story begins in Ireland and Scotland, with the Gaels, a Celtic people. Their year had two halves: a light half and a dark half. And the doorway between them was a festival called Samhain, on the first of November. It marked the end of the harvest. Cattle were brought down from the summer pastures, food was stored, and some animals were slaughtered for the winter. Here's the key detail: for the Celts, a day began at sunset, not at midnight. So Samhain started on the evening of October thirty-first. That's why Halloween is a night, not a day. One honest caveat: the druids left no writing. Most of what we know comes from medieval Irish tales, written down centuries later by Christian monks.

In those tales, Samhain is when the wall between our world and the Otherworld grows thin. The fairy mounds open up, and spirits, fairies and the souls of the dead walk among the living. Some came looking for a warm hearth. Others came looking for trouble. So people protected themselves. They lit bonfires on the hills. They left food and drink outside for the wandering dead. And later, in Scotland and Ireland, young people went guising: they put on masks and disguises and went from house to house. The idea was simple: if a spirit couldn't recognize you, it couldn't take you. That's the oldest root of the Halloween costume.

Then came Christianity. In the eighth century, Pope Gregory the Third dedicated a chapel in Rome to all the saints, with a feast on the first of November. About a hundred years later, the date spread across the Church. Historians still argue whether this was a deliberate move to replace Samhain, but the result was the same. The first of November became All Saints' Day, also called All Hallows, from the old English word for holy. Soon the second of November became All Souls' Day, for everyone who had died. And the evening before All Hallows was All Hallows' Even. Say it fast enough, for a few hundred years, and you get Hallowe'en. Then Halloween.

The Church also gave us the first version of trick-or-treating. In medieval Britain, on these days, the poor went door to door asking for soul cakes: small round cakes, often marked with a cross. In return, they promised to pray for the souls of the family's dead. It was called souling, and it was so familiar that Shakespeare mentions it: a character whines like a beggar at Hallowmas. So, picture it: kids, costumes, knocking on doors, getting a sweet treat. The pieces were already there. They just hadn't come together yet.

Now, the lanterns. In Ireland, there's an old legend about a man called Stingy Jack. Jack tricked the Devil, more than once. In one version, he talks the Devil into climbing an apple tree, then carves crosses into the trunk, so the Devil can't come down until he promises never to take Jack's soul. When Jack finally dies, Heaven won't let in a man like him. And Hell won't take him either: a deal is a deal. So the Devil throws him a single burning coal, and Jack puts it inside a hollowed-out turnip to light his way. Ever since, he's been wandering the dark: Jack of the lantern. People in Ireland and Scotland carved scary faces into turnips, potatoes and beets, and put them in windows to keep Jack and other wandering spirits away. And in Scotland, people bobbed for apples and played fortune-telling games. Robert Burns even wrote a whole poem about it, called Halloween, in seventeen eighty-five.

So how did all of this end up in America? Not with the Pilgrims. The Puritans of New England disliked holidays like this, so for a long time Halloween barely existed there. It was more common in Maryland and the southern colonies. Then, in eighteen forty-five, a disease destroyed Ireland's potato crop. The Great Famine killed about a million people, and around two million more left the country, many of them for America. They brought their customs with them. And in America, they found a vegetable that was native there: the pumpkin. Bigger, softer, and much easier to carve than a turnip. By the eighteen-sixties, the carved pumpkin was a Halloween symbol.

By the late eighteen hundreds, Halloween in America was mostly a party for adults: apple games, ghost stories, and fortune-telling about who you'd marry. But on the streets, it was a night of pranks. Gates disappeared, windows got soaped, outhouses were tipped over. By the nineteen-twenties and thirties, during the Great Depression, the pranks turned into real vandalism. So towns tried something new: organized parties, parades, and kids going house to house for treats, so they'd be too busy to cause trouble. Around this time, a new phrase starts appearing in print. One of the earliest known examples comes from a newspaper in Alberta, Canada, in nineteen twenty-seven: trick or treat.

Then World War Two hit. Sugar was rationed in the United States from nineteen forty-two, and trick-or-treating almost disappeared. But after the war, everything lined up: a baby boom, new suburbs full of kids, and candy companies eager to sell. By the mid-fifties, magazines were full of Halloween candy ads. Pop culture helped too: Donald Duck starred in a cartoon called Trick or Treat in nineteen fifty-two, and in nineteen sixty-six, Charlie Brown waited all night for the Great Pumpkin. And what about the famous poisoned candy scare? Researchers who studied it found almost no real cases of strangers poisoning kids' treats. Still, it pushed everyone toward factory-sealed, individually wrapped candy.

And that brings us to today. About thirteen and a half billion dollars a year in the United States, roughly a hundred and fifteen dollars per person. Costumes are the biggest slice at four point four billion, then decorations, then candy. Americans even spend around three quarters of a billion dollars just on pumpkins. And the holiday has now traveled back across the ocean: Ireland and Britain, where it all began, celebrate an American-style Halloween. So the next time you carve a pumpkin or open the door to a tiny skeleton, remember: you're keeping alive a chain that goes back more than a thousand years: from Celtic bonfires, to soul cakes, to a stingy man with a turnip. Our ancestors dressed up to hide from the dead. Now, we dress up as them.
